part1_page.title: CS2 Week 11 -- Optional Micro-Lab: Benchmark and Tell the Story
part1_page.body:
Optional micro-lab: benchmark sorting and searching, then tell the story

Optional and experimental. The required Week 11 work is unchanged: Honest Visualization from Project Data and its Reasoning Odyssey gate. This is a ready-made dataset you may use for the same gate if your own project data is thin, or just to see your own machine's numbers.

The idea

Week 9 said bubble sort grows like n² and Python's sort is fast. Measure it on your machine (Windows, WSL, Linux, or Mac) and decide what a reader should believe. Different machines give different numbers. Is the story the same?

Run it (1–2 minutes)

Download: benchmark.py, plot_benchmark.py, and sample_results.csv (an example run, so you can try the charts first). Put them in one folder, then:

python benchmark.py --quick          # a few seconds, sanity check
python benchmark.py                  # full run, writes results_<your-host>.csv
python -m pip install matplotlib     # once, if needed
python plot_benchmark.py results_<your-host>.csv --outdir charts

On Windows use py -3 if python is not found; on WSL/Linux/Mac use python3. Each CSV row carries a platform fingerprint (OS, Python version, CPU count). No username goes inside the file; the hostname is only in the file name, so rename it before sharing if you like.

It times bubble, insertion, merge, and built-in sorted, plus linear, binary, and library bisect search, over several list sizes and orderings. Times are best-of-several using time.perf_counter().

The story to tell (fits the Week 11 gate)

  • Question — one answerable question, e.g. “How much faster is binary than linear search at 100,000 items on my machine?”
  • Visual — one labeled chart (axis labels with units, a title that states a claim, a legend).
  • Rationale — why these axes. Log-log is honest here because growth rate is the point.
  • Limitation — one run, one machine, background programs, best-of-N timing, capped n; built-in sorted is C code, the others are Python. Claim no cause you did not test.
  • Evidence — your CSV, the command you ran, and 3_PITFALL_linear_axis.png named as the misleading alternative with one sentence on what it hides.

The harness ships the pitfall: the same data on linear axes from zero, where the two slow sorts set the scale and the fast ones are squashed against the bottom. Explain why chart 1 is the honest one.

Share and compare

Post your chart, a one-paragraph story, and your platform line in the discussion: Week 11 optional micro-lab: share your benchmark chart. Read at least two classmates' posts and compare what changed between machines and what stayed the same. Post nothing private (no usernames, no paths with your name).

Honest cautions

  • Timings are noisy. Close other programs; run twice if a number looks odd.
  • Compare the same algorithm across machines, not a hand-written sort against sorted.
  • “Binary search was about 1,000x faster here at n = 100,000” is a claim. “Linux is faster than Windows” is not.

Part 2: The Story of Big O — count what the sort actually does, graph it, and compare algorithms.
